Bushel
BOOSH-el
noun
From the Old French boissel, a small box or measure, through Low Latin bustellus; in the Authorized Version it renders the Greek modios, the dry measure of about a peck, and by extension the vessel that held it.

Biblical Definition

A bushel is a dry measure and the vessel that contains it — a common household tub, wide enough and deep enough to cover a burning lamp and put out its light. Our Lord uses it three times, and always in the same argument: “Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house” (Mat 5:15). The point is not the measure but the absurdity. No man kindles a flame in order to hide it; the very act of lighting declares an intention that it be seen. Mark adds a second hiding place, the bed, and puts the whole in the form of a question the disciples must answer for themselves (Mar 4:21); Luke adds the secret place and names the purpose plainly, “that they which come in may see the light” (Luk 11:33). The candle is not the believer’s own light. Christ is the light of the world (Joh 8:12), and the church shines only as the moon shines. But the borrowed light is real light, and it was given for a house full of people. Therefore the visibility of the church is not vanity but obedience: let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven (Mat 5:16). A hidden Christian is a contradiction of the purpose for which he was lit.

Webster 1828 Definition

A dry measure of eight gallons, and the vessel holding it; in the Gospels the covering under which no man puts a lighted candle.

expand to see more

BUSHEL, n. [Old French boissel; Low Latin bustellus, a little box.] A dry measure containing eight gallons or four pecks.

Also, the vessel or tub in which that quantity is measured.

In the New Testament it renders the Greek modios, a measure of about a peck.

Figuratively, whatever conceals or smothers what was meant to be seen.

To hide one’s light under a bushel is proverbial in English from Matthew 5:15.

Key Scripture

Mat 5:15 — "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house."

Mar 4:21 — "And he said unto them, Is a candle brought to be put under a bushel, or under a bed? and not to be set on a candlestick?"

Luk 11:33 — "No man, when he hath lighted a candle, putteth it in a secret place, neither under a bushel, but on a candlestick, that they which come in may see the light."

Mat 5:14 — "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid."

Modern Corruption

The saying is bent into a self-esteem slogan about unused talent, and, at the other extreme, into a warrant for a church that hides its doctrine to keep the world’s goodwill.

expand to see more

Two opposite misuses run at once. The first empties the text of God: “don’t hide your light under a bushel” is quoted at graduations and in motivational speech to mean that a man should display his gifts and not be modest about them. That is the exact reverse of the sentence following, which orders the light shown so that men glorify the Father and not the lamp. The second misuse is quieter and does more damage in the churches: a ministry that trims what it confesses, keeps its doctrine off its website, and speaks of sin only in words the world cannot take offence at — and calls this wisdom. It is the bushel, however carefully carpentered. The Lord did not say the candle should be set where none may stumble over it; He said it should be set where all in the house may see it. A church ashamed of the whole counsel of God has not become winsome; it has gone out.

Recover the purpose clause. The candle is lit for the house, and the house is full of people who came in out of the dark. What must be seen is good works — a life ordered by God’s law, a marriage kept, a word kept, wages paid, the poor cared for — and the doctrine that produced them, so that the glory lands where it belongs. Visibility is not self-promotion when the light is borrowed and the praise is redirected. Take the tub off. Let the neighbours know what you believe and see how you live, and leave the glorifying to God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

A dry measure and its tub; the Gospel figure for anything that smothers the light Christ kindled to be seen.

expand to see more

Bushel — Old French boissel, a little box; Low Latin bustellus.

Greek modios, a dry measure of about a peck and the vessel that held it.

Three Gospel occurrences, all of the same saying: Mat 5:15; Mar 4:21; Luk 11:33.

Paired always with the candlestick — the wrong place against the right one.

Mark adds the bed, Luke the secret place: the ways of hiding are many, the lamp is one.

Usage

"The saying is about the church’s witness, not about a man’s unused abilities."

"Mat 5:16 supplies the purpose: that they may glorify your Father, not admire you."

"A doctrine kept quiet for the sake of reputation is a bushel by another name."
